posts.text:
England executed a king in 1649. Eleven years later it invited his son back to be king again. This is the story in between.

a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ Charles I lost the argument for good on 30 January 1649, beheaded outside the Banqueting House at Whitehall — still the only time an English monarch has been tried and executed by his own state.
2/ England abolished the monarchy entirely and became the Commonwealth. For the first time in its history, the answer to 'who is king' was nobody.
3/ Charles's exiled son didn't give up. Crowned King of Scots in 1651, he invaded England with a Scottish army — and was crushed by Cromwell at the Battle of Worcester on 3 September 1651.

4/ Charles II spent about six weeks afterward as a fugitive in his own country, reportedly hiding at one point in an oak tree while Parliamentarian soldiers searched below, before escaping to France in disguise.
5/ Oliver Cromwell ran the republic as Lord Protector until his death in 1658. His son Richard inherited the job and lasted less than a year before the army eased him out.

6/ By 1660, with no workable alternative left, Parliament invited Charles II home. He landed at Dover that May and was crowned — the monarchy restored after an eleven-year gap that started with an execution and ended with an invitation.
7/ We go deeper on how England got to the execution in the first place — the newsletter has the full year-by-year breakdown: https://buttondown.com/forummapping
